宣德五年進士登科錄

玉音

宣德五年二月十九日早，行在禮部尚書胡濙等官於奉天門奏，為科舉事：會試天下舉人，選中一百名。本年三月十五日，請讀卷及執事等官：少師兼吏部尚書蹇義、少傅兵部尚書兼華蓋殿大學士臣楊士奇等四十一員。其進士出身等第，恭依祖高皇帝欽定資格：第一甲例取三名，第一名從六品，第二、第三名正七品，賜進士及第；第二甲從七品，賜進士出身；第三甲正八品，賜同進士出身。奉聖旨：「是。欽此。」

讀卷官
榮祿大夫、少師兼吏部尚書蹇義〔乙丑進士〕
榮祿大夫、少傅、兵部尚書兼華蓋殿大學士楊士奇
translation_en:
Record of the Metropolitan Graduates of the Fifth Year of the Xuande Reign (Xuande wunian jinshi dengke lu)

Imperial Pronouncement (Yuyin)

Early on the nineteenth day of the second month of the fifth year of the Xuande reign [March 13, 1430], Hu Ying 胡濙, Minister of Rites in the Auxiliary Administration, and other officials submitted a memorial at the Fengtian Gate concerning the civil service examinations: In the Metropolitan Examination of provincial graduates (juren) from across the empire, one hundred men have been selected. On the fifteenth day of the third month of the present year [April 7, 1430], we request the appointment of Readers of Examination Papers and officiating officials, namely the Junior Preceptor and concurrent Minister of Personnel Jian Yi 蹇義, the Junior Guardian, Minister of War, and concurrent Grand Secretary of the Huagai Hall, Your servant Yang Shiqi 楊士奇, and others, forty-one officials in all. As for the grades of qualification for the metropolitan graduates (jinshi), we respectfully follow the ranks imperially established by the Progenitor, the Exalted Emperor [the Hongwu Emperor]: for the First Class (jia), three men are taken according to precedent, the first to be accorded rank 6b and the second and third rank 7a, all bestowed the title "Metropolitan Graduate with Honors" (jinshi jidi); those of the Second Class are to be accorded rank 7b and bestowed the title "Metropolitan Graduate" (jinshi chushen); those of the Third Class are to be accorded rank 8a and bestowed the title "Associate Metropolitan Graduate" (tong jinshi chushen). We received the Imperial Edict: "Approved. Respect this."

Readers of Examination Papers (Dujuan guan)
Jian Yi 蹇義, Grandee of the Sixteenth Class, Junior Preceptor, and concurrent Minister of Personnel (Metropolitan Graduate of the yichou year [1385]).
Yang Shiqi 楊士奇, Grandee of the Sixteenth Class, Junior Guardian, Minister of War, and concurrent Grand Secretary of the Huagai Hall.

三月十七日早，文武百官朝服侍班。是日，行在錦衣衛設鹵簿于丹陛、丹墀內，上御奉天殿，行在鴻臚寺官傳制唱名。行在禮部官捧黃榜，鼓樂導引，出長安左門外張掛。畢，順天府官用傘蓋儀從送狀元歸第。
translation_en:
Sequence of Imperial Honors
Fifth Year of the Xuande Reign (1430)
Early in the morning on the fifteenth day of the third month, the tribute scholars (gongshi) proceeded to the Inner Palace for the Palace Examination, where His Majesty took his seat in the Hall of Appealing to Heaven (Fengtian dian) and personally posed the policy question.
Early in the morning on the seventeenth day of the third month, all civil and military officials stood in attendance in court dress. On this day, the Embroidered-uniform Guard in the Auxiliary Administration set up the imperial insignia arrays upon the Cinnabar Steps and within the Cinnabar Courtyard. His Majesty took his seat in the Hall of Appealing to Heaven, and officials of the Court of State Ceremonial in the Auxiliary Administration transmitted the Emperor's decree and called out the names on the roll. Officials of the Ministry of Rites in the Auxiliary Administration held up the yellow placard, and, led by drums and music, went out past the Left Chang'an Gate to post it on display. Once this was completed, officials of Shuntian Prefecture used a ceremonial parasol and retinue to escort the Principal Graduate (zhuangyuan) back to his residence.

李淳〔貫山西平陽府曲沃縣，民籍，河南歸德州學生，治《書經》，字宗元，行一，年三十四，十一月初一日生〕。曾祖添祥，祖從政，父溥〔任歸德州儒學訓導〕，母吉氏，繼母郭氏。慈侍下。弟靜、武、文。娶田氏。河南鄉試第五名，會試第十二名。

Fan Rong 范鎔, registered in a military household in Linchuan County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, is a Student of the Directorate of Imperial Academy specializing in the Book of Documents (Shujing); his courtesy name is Jiuding, he is the second son in his generation, is thirty-five sui, and was born on the sixth day of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was Renqing, his grandfather was Zhongxiang, his father is Qizong, and his mother is née Huang. Both of his parents are living. His younger paternal cousins are Jiuchou, Longsun, and Xianshou; he is married to a woman née Zhou. He placed 112th in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 69th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Yu 王玉, registered in a military household in Wucheng County, Gaotang Subprefecture, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong, is a Student of the Yizhou Subprefectural School specializing in the Book of Changes (Yijing); his courtesy name is Tingqi, he is the third son in his generation, is twenty-nine sui, and was born on the second day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Shenggang, a Company Commander (baihu) under the Yuan dynasty; his grandfather was Cheng, posthumously honored as Vice Director in the Ministry of Works; his father is Shijia, serving as Director of a Bureau in the Ministry of Works; and his mother is née Sang, invested as Lady of Suitability (yiren). Both of his parents are living. His elder brothers are Ziying and Zijie, a Prefectural Instructor of Divination (yinyang xunshu), and his younger brother is Zixing; he is married to a woman née Song. He placed 2nd in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 44th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Chun 李淳, registered in a civilian household in Quwo County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, is a Student of the Guide Subprefectural School in Henan specializing in the Book of Documents (Shujing); his courtesy name is Zongyuan, he is the first son in his generation, is thirty-four sui, and was born on the first day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Tianxiang; his grandfather was Congzheng; his father was Pu, who served as Assistant Instructor in the Guide Subprefectural Confucian School; his mother was née Ji; and his stepmother is née Guo. His stepmother is living and his father is deceased. His younger brothers are Jing, Wu, and Wen; he is married to a woman née Tian. He placed 5th in the Henan Provincial Examination and 12th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiao Weizhen 蕭維禎, registered in a civilian household in Luling County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi, is a County School Student specializing in the Book of Odes (Shijing); his courtesy name is Weizhen, he is the first son in his generation, is twenty-five sui, and was born on the sixteenth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Fuxin, his grandfather is Lecun, his father is Bumin, and his mother is née Zhou. Both his grandparents and his parents are living. His younger brothers are Jing and Lun, and his younger paternal cousins are Ji and Yun; he is married to a woman née Liu. He placed 17th in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 13th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 宣德五年進士登科錄
text:
臣林震
臣對臣聞致治之道必以教養為先而教養之
道當以得人為要盖農桑所以養民學校所以
教民是二者衣食之本風化之源而君人者不
可不以此為先務也昔孔子之論治道曰既富
矣而必曰教之孟子之論三政必以均田制與
學校而為說者夫豈無徵之空言哉然非得人
亦無以行之故又曰為政在人焉洪惟
太祖高皇帝肇造鴻業
太宗文皇帝中興家邦
===
仁宗昭皇帝恭已守成
聖聖相繼實同一心其重農事而田制有等則之均
崇教化而内外有學校之建方今
皇上嗣登寶位勵精圖理乃進臣等于

臣林震。

臣對：臣聞致治之道，必以教養為先，而教養之道，當以得人為要。盖農桑所以養民，學校所以教民，是二者，衣食之本、風化之源，而君人者不可不以此為先務也。昔孔子之論治道，曰「既富矣」，而必曰「教之」；孟子之論三政，必以均田制、與學校而為說者，夫豈無徵之空言哉！然非得人，亦無以行之，故又曰「為政在人」焉。洪惟太祖高皇帝肇造鴻業，太宗文皇帝中興家邦，仁宗昭皇帝恭已守成，聖聖相繼，實同一心。其重農事而田制有等則之均，崇教化而内外有學校之建。方今皇上嗣登寶位，勵精圖理，乃進臣等于廷，降賜清問，遠舉唐、虞、三代教養之道，近述祖宗列聖勤民之政，且自期以咸躋雍熙而恪謹繼述。臣有以知皇上是心，即祖宗列聖之心也，即堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之心也。臣雖愚
translation_en:
Your servant Lin Zhen 林震.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that in the way of achieving good governance, one must put education and nourishment first, and in the way of education and nourishment, one ought to take obtaining capable men as the essential point. For agriculture and sericulture are the means to nourish the people, and schools are the means to educate the people. These two are the foundation of food and clothing and the source of moral transformation, and one who rules over men cannot but take them as his foremost task. In antiquity, when Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) discussed the way of governance, after saying "Once they are enriched," he invariably said "Educate them." When Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) discussed kingly governance [?; 三政 for 王政], he invariably expounded upon equalizing the land system and establishing [?; 與 for 興] schools—how could these be unsubstantiated empty words! Yet without obtaining capable men, there is no way to put them into practice; therefore it is also said, "Governance lies in the men."

Humbly reflecting upon how Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao (Taizu Gao Huangdi 太祖高皇帝) first founded the great enterprise, Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen (Taizong Wen Huangdi 太宗文皇帝) revived the dynastic state, and Benevolent Ancestor Emperor Zhao (Renzong Zhao Huangdi 仁宗昭皇帝) reverently maintained the achievements—sage succeeding sage, truly sharing a single mind—they valued agriculture so that the land system had an equitable gradation of rates, and they esteemed moral transformation so that schools were established both in the capital and in the provinces. Now Your Majesty has succeeded to the precious throne and strives with utmost vigor for good governance. You have summoned your servants to the court and graciously bestowed Your pure inquiry, citing from afar the way of education and nourishment in the times of Tang 唐, Yu 虞, and the Three Dynasties, and recounting from recent times the governance of diligent care for the people by the Imperial Ancestors and successive sages, while expecting of Yourself to raise all to harmonious prosperity and to be reverently prudent in continuing and carrying forward their work. Your servant thereby knows that this mind of Your Majesty is none other than the mind of the Imperial Ancestors and successive sages, and none other than the mind of Yao 堯, Shun 舜, Yu 禹, Tang 湯, Wen 文, and Wu 武. Though your servant is foolish…

聖天子之休命乎臣聞自古帝王為治之道不越乎

…and rustic, how dare I not devote my heart in pure sincerity to respond to and extol the illustrious mandate of the Sacred Son of Heaven?

Your servant has heard that since antiquity, the Way by which emperors and kings have governed does not go beyond instruction and nourishment alone. Nourishment is the means to enrich the people's livelihood, and instruction is the means to perfect the people's nature; when both are carried out together, the Way of governance is complete. Thus, when Yao rose specifically from being Marquis of Tang to become Emperor, his ways of achieving good governance were certainly not limited to a single aspect, yet he necessarily first commanded Ji and Xie to take up the offices of instruction and nourishment. When Shun, with his double brilliance, succeeded Yao in achieving good governance, his benevolent policies toward the people were likewise not limited to a single matter, yet he necessarily renewed the commands to Ji and Xie to "sow in season the hundred grains" and "reverently propagate the Five Teachings." Therefore, in the times of Tang and Yu, every family was provided for and every person had enough, so that every household side by side was worthy of enfeoffment—this indeed had its origin.

Coming down to the successive rise of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou, for nourishing the people they had policies regarding fields and property, and for instructing the people they had policies regarding schools. What the commentary refers to as "under the Xia-hou clan, fifty mu and the tribute (gong) system; under the Yin people, seventy mu and the aid (zhu) system; under the Zhou people, one hundred mu and the share (che) system"—though the institutions differed, in reality all were a tithe of one-tenth, and were nothing other than the means to nourish the people. What it refers to as "the Xia called them jiao, the Yin called them xu, and the Zhou called them xiang, while xue was shared by all Three Dynasties"—though the names were not uniform, all served to clarify human relationships, and were nothing other than the means to instruct the people. Therefore, in the times of the Three Dynasties, governance was flourishing and customs were admirable, and everyone possessed the conduct of scholars and noble men—how could this have been without a foundation?

Yet this Way has been inherited in succession by the Illustrious Sages of our State. Over the course of more than sixty years, the realm has enjoyed Great Peace and the Four Seas have been tranquil. Going out to work at daybreak and coming in to rest at nightfall, the people are joyful in the abundance of full stomachs and warm clothes; with fathers compassionate and sons filial, they flourish within the transformative teaching of rites and music. 皇上宵旰孜孜於教養之務尤加之意焉故愛民若
保赤子則心之愛者誠矣而田里未皆給足教
化本於躬行則謹諸己者至矣而風俗未底刑
措此非
皇上之心有所未盡也殆承流宣化職任師儒者之
未盡得其人也盖知人之實自古為難
太宗八難未甞不審然論篤者未免為色莊靜
言者每至於庸違才優於趙魏老者又不可以
為滕薛大夫也□而

黄卓魯之輩則戶口增田野闢而烝民莫不粒
食矣何患田里之未皆給足乎職任學校者皆
如胡瑗之教蘇湖則教化行善人多而風俗莫

translation_en:
…surpassed that of the Three Dynasties. Down to Your Majesty, who works tirelessly from before dawn until after dark, you pay especial attention to the tasks of instruction and nourishment. Thus, in loving the people as if protecting a newborn infant, the love in your heart is truly sincere, yet the fields and villages are not all amply provided for; in basing moral transformation upon personal practice, your self-cultivation is truly complete, yet customs have not reached the point where punishments can be set aside. This is not because Your Majesty's heart has left anything undone; rather, it is probably because those who transmit the sovereign's grace and propagate moral transformation, and those who hold the offices of instructors and Confucian scholars, are not all the right men. Indeed, the reality of truly knowing men has been difficult since antiquity. Although Tang Taizong's唐太宗 eight difficulties in judging men were not without careful discernment, those whose discourse is earnest may turn out to be merely putting on a grave countenance; those who speak smoothly often end up acting perversely when employed; and one whose talent is more than sufficient to serve as a steward of the Zhao 趙 or Wei 魏 noble houses still cannot be made a Grand Master of the small states of Teng 滕 or Xue 薛. [?] Yet if Your Majesty can truly select with care the officials of the Ministry of Personnel and impartially carry out the laws of selection and appointment, and cautiously choose those entrusted with Censorial duties while striving to fulfill the reality of impeachment and surveillance—causing Commandery Governors and District Magistrates all to be like men such as Gong Sui 龔遂, Huang Ba 黄霸, Zhuo Mao 卓茂, and Lu Gong 魯恭—then households and population will increase, fields and wilds will be opened up for cultivation, and the multitude of the people will all have grain to eat. What worry would there be that the fields and villages are not all amply provided for? If those holding office in the schools are all like Hu Yuan 胡瑗 when he taught in Suzhou 蘇州 and Huzhou 湖州, then moral transformation will prevail, good men will be numerous, and customs will all be greatly transformed. What worry would there be that the realm has not reached the point where punishments can be set aside?

Your servant is a lowly scholar from the rustic wilds, and my study of the learning that illuminates fundamental principles and applies them to practical use is not yet thorough. Since Your Majesty, in putting this policy question to your servant, wished me to set forth the essentials that can be put into practice, your servant therefore dares, at the risk of death, to present to Your Majesty the argument that obtaining the right men is the essential point. Humbly I pray that…

清問遠稽唐虞三代教養之法欲行之今日以臻
乎治效之隆臣有以見
陛下不自滿足之心詢于芻蕘之意也臣敢不拜手
稽首以對揚
punctuated:
臣龔錡。
臣對：臣聞農桑學校，王政之所先；任賢使能，君道之當務。盖賢才者，人君資之以輔治者也。賢才用於上，則治效著於下，安有農桑之不舉、學校之不脩乎？是知為治固在於教養，而教養又在於得人也。欽惟太祖高皇帝肇造鴻業，撫有六合；太宗文皇帝紹承大統，中興邦家。列聖相承，嗣膺寶圖，恭己守成，重農事，崇學校，其法精備，超邁古昔。皇上嗣天位，纘大烈，循治古之良規，継述之美，有光于前。歌鳳儀獸舞之治者，莫不沐浴其膏澤；樂鳶飛魚躍之天者，靡不漸摩乎仁義。而猶曰田里未皆給足，風俗未底刑措，乃進臣等於廷，降賜清問，遠稽唐、虞、三代教養之法，欲行之今日，以臻乎治效之隆。臣有以見陛下不自滿足之心，詢于芻蕘之意也。臣敢不拜手稽首，以對揚…
translation_en:
Your servant Gong Qi 龔錡.
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that agriculture, sericulture, and schools are what kingly governance puts first, and that employing the worthy and engaging the capable are the proper duties of the ruler's way. For worthy talents are those upon whom a ruler relies to assist in governance. When worthy talents are employed above, the results of good governance become manifest below—how could agriculture and sericulture not be promoted, or schools not be maintained? From this we know that while governing assuredly lies in education and nourishment, education and nourishment in turn lie in obtaining the right people. Your servant reverently reflects that the Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu Gao Huangdi 太祖高皇帝), founded the great enterprise and pacified and possessed the six directions; the Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong Wen Huangdi 太宗文皇帝), succeeded to the great succession and revitalized the state. Successive sacred emperors followed one another in receiving the precious mandate; holding themselves in reverent self-restraint to preserve what had been achieved, they emphasized agriculture and revered schools, their institutions refined and complete, surpassing those of antiquity. Your Majesty has succeeded to the Heavenly Throne and carried on the great meritorious achievements, following the fine regulations of well-governed antiquity; the beauty of your continuation and transmission adds luster to your predecessors. Those who sing of a reign in which phoenixes come with stately gait and beasts dance in harmony are all bathed in its enriching grace; those who rejoice under a sky where hawks soar and fishes leap are all imbued with benevolence and righteousness. Yet You still say that the fields and villages are not all sufficiently provided for, and that customs have not yet reached the point where punishments can be set aside. Thus You have brought your servants forward into the court and graciously bestowed Your pure inquiry, looking far back to the methods of education and nourishment of Tang 唐, Yu 虞, and the Three Dynasties (Sandai 三代), wishing to put them into practice today so as to reach the pinnacle of effective governance. Your servant is thereby able to perceive Your Majesty's mind that does not rest content with itself, and Your intention to consult even grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers. How could your servant dare not bow with clasped hands and knock his head to the ground to respond and extol…

聖策所及而陳之夫養民莫重於授田教民莫先於

punctuated: 明天子之休命乎！臣謹因聖策所及而陳之。夫養民莫重於授田，教民莫先於建學。非制田里以養民，則無以遂其生；非建學校以教民，則無以復其性。大哉，教養之道乎！其所以為治天下之要道乎！粤稽諸古，大舜紹堯致治，恭己無為，命稷以播百穀，五穀熟而人民育；命契以敷五教，五教明而風俗美。迨夫三代，受田建學，亦無不備。以其授田而言，夏后氏五十而貢，殷人七十而助，至周則通用貢助之法，百畝之徹；以其建學而言，夏有東序、西序，商有左學、右學，至周則法制加詳焉。是以唐、虞、三代之民，出作入息，不知帝力之加，敏德遷善，而造皇極之域。治化之盛，誠非後世之所能及也。洪惟陛下法祖為治，而用人尤謹。屢勅有司，治尚寬仁，脩舉政事，蓋欲任牧守者皆如龔、黄、卓、魯，而養民之心無以加；簡擇生徒，選任學官，蓋欲為師表者皆如周、程、張、朱，而教民之意無以尚。家給人足而九敘惟歌，教化大行而刑措不用，於今而見之。然
translation_en:
… the beneficent mandate of the enlightened Son of Heaven? Your servant respectfully sets forth his views in accordance with what Your Sacred Policy Question has touched upon.

Now, in nourishing the people, nothing is more important than allotting land; in educating the people, nothing takes precedence over establishing schools. Without regulating fields and homesteads to nourish the people, there is no means for them to fulfill their livelihoods; without establishing schools to educate the people, there is no means for them to recover their innate nature. Great indeed is the Way of educating and nourishing! Is it not the essential Way for governing all under heaven?

Examining antiquity, Great Shun succeeded Yao in achieving good governance. Holding himself in reverence and acting through non-purposive action, he commanded Ji 稷 to sow the hundred grains, so that the five grains ripened and the people were nourished; he commanded Xie 契 to propagate the five teachings, so that the five teachings were made clear and customs became admirable. Coming down to the Three Dynasties, the allotment of land and the establishment of schools were likewise complete in every respect. Speaking of their allotment of land, the Xia dynasty allotted fifty mu and used the tribute system (gong), the Yin people allotted seventy mu and used the mutual-aid system (zhu), and by the Zhou they combined the tribute and mutual-aid methods into the hundred-mu tithing system (che). Speaking of their establishment of schools, the Xia had the Eastern Xu and Western Xu, the Shang had the Left School and Right School, and by the Zhou the institutional regulations became even more detailed. Therefore, the people of the Tang, Yu, and Three Dynasties went out to work and came in to rest, unaware of the sovereign's exertion on their behalf; they were diligent in virtue and moved toward goodness, reaching the realm of Supreme Perfection (huangji). The flourishing of their governance and transformation is truly something later ages have been unable to match.

I humbly reflect that Your Majesty models your governance upon the Imperial Ancestors, and is especially prudent in employing men. You have repeatedly commanded the authorities to esteem leniency and benevolence in governance and to put administrative affairs in order, desiring that those appointed as regional governors and prefects should all be like Gong Sui 龔遂, Huang Ba 黄霸, Zhuo Mao 卓茂, and Lu Gong 魯恭, so that nothing could surpass your heart in nourishing the people; you have selected students with care and appointed Confucian school officials, desiring that those who serve as models and teachers should all be like Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤, the Cheng brothers 程 (Cheng Hao 程顥 and Cheng Yi 程頤), Zhang Zai 張載, and Zhu Xi 朱熹, so that nothing could exceed your intention in educating the people. Every household is well-supplied and every person content, so that the nine divisions of administration are all celebrated in song; moral transformation prevails widely and punishments are set aside unused—this is witnessed today. Yet…

punctuated: 猶策臣，謂别有其道。臣以為法祖、用賢之外，豈復有他道哉？臣於終篇，願有獻焉。盖心者，萬化之原、萬事之本，而治道之所由出也。前聖之重農事、崇學校者，此心也；陛下誠心以愛民、躬行以率下者，亦此心也。臣願陛下終始此心，終始此道，則終始此治，唐、虞、三代之盛，端在於今日矣。臣不揣凡庸，敢陳愚見，惟陛下不勝怖懼之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: … you still put this policy question to your servant, asking whether there is some other Way. Your servant holds that beyond emulating the Imperial Ancestors and employing the worthy, how could there be any other Way? At the conclusion of this essay, your servant wishes to offer a further word. For the mind is the source of the myriad transformations, the root of the myriad affairs, and that from which the Way of governance springs. When the former sages emphasized agriculture and venerated schools, it was out of this mind; when Your Majesty loves the people with a sincere mind and leads subordinates through personal practice, it is likewise out of this mind. Your servant prays that Your Majesty will maintain this mind from beginning to end, and maintain this Way from beginning to end; then you will maintain this good governance from beginning to end, and the flourishing of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties will truly be realized today! Looking solely to Your Majesty [? text missing after 陛下, e.g., 裁擇焉], your servant is overcome with the utmost trepidation. Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 宣德五年進士登科錄
text:
臣林文
臣對臣聞為治之道莫先於教養教養之政莫
先於得賢蓋民非養則無以厚其生非教則無
以復其性苟不得賢以行教養之政又安能盡
為治之道哉自古帝王體天致治任君師之寄
者未嘗不以教養為先得賢為要也欽惟
皇上稟聰明睿智之資備聖神文武之德膺
天命之隆眷嗣
洪業孜孜焉以養民為心切切焉以教民為
務天所覆□所載無一夫而不遂其耕食
===
飲之樂日月□照霜露所墜無一人而不遂
父慈子孝之□治已洽矣而猶慮其未洽民
已安矣而猶慮其未安復進臣等於
廷而以唐虞三代教養為問臣知
皇上是心即堯舜禹湯文武之心欲使斯民為唐虞
三代之民也臣敢不精白一心以對揚
聖天子之休命乎粵稽有虞之君紹陶唐之治慮百
姓之阻饑也則命稷為田正之官播時百穀使
斯民皆得其養慮百姓之不親也則命契典司
徒之職敬敷五教使斯民皆復其性當是時也

務天所覆地所載無一夫而不遂其耕食
===

父慈子孝之天治已洽矣而猶慮其未洽民
已安矣而猶慮其未安復進臣等於

皇上是心即堯舜禹湯文武之心欲使斯民爲唐虞

斯民皆得其養慮百姓之不親也則命契典司
徒之職敬敷五教使斯民皆復其性當是時也
punctuated:
臣林文。
臣對：臣聞為治之道，莫先於教養；教養之政，莫先於得賢。蓋民非養則無以厚其生，非教則無以復其性；苟不得賢以行教養之政，又安能盡為治之道哉？自古帝王體天致治，任君師之寄者，未嘗不以教養為先、得賢為要也。欽惟皇上稟聰明睿智之資，備聖神文武之德，膺天命之隆眷，嗣洪業，孜孜焉以養民為心，切切焉以教民為務。天所覆、□所載，無一夫而不遂其耕食飲之樂；日月□照、霜露所墜，無一人而不遂父慈子孝之□。治已洽矣，而猶慮其未洽；民已安矣，而猶慮其未安。復進臣等於廷，而以唐、虞、三代教養為問。臣知皇上是心，即堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之心，欲使斯民為唐、虞、三代之民也。臣敢不精白一心，以對揚聖天子之休命乎？粵稽有虞之君，紹陶唐之治，慮百姓之阻饑也，則命稷為田正之官，播時百穀，使斯民皆得其養；慮百姓之不親也，則命契典司徒之職，敬敷五教，使斯民皆復其性。當是時也，
translation_en:
Your servant Lin Wen 林文.
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that in the Way of governance, nothing takes precedence over instruction and nourishment; and in the administration of instruction and nourishment, nothing takes precedence over obtaining worthy men. For if the people are not nourished, there is no means to enrich their livelihood; if they are not instructed, there is no means to restore their innate nature. Yet if one does not obtain worthy men to carry out the administration of instruction and nourishment, how then can one fulfill the Way of governance? Since antiquity, emperors and kings who embodied Heaven to bring about order and bore the responsibilities of ruler and teacher have never failed to place instruction and nourishment first, and to regard obtaining worthy men as essential.
I reverently reflect that Your Majesty, endowed with the natural gifts of keen perception and profound wisdom, possessing the virtues of sageliness, divinity, civil accomplishment, and martial vigor, has received the abundant favor of the Mandate of Heaven and succeeded to the Great Enterprise. Tirelessly, You take nourishing the people as Your heart's concern; earnestly, You take instructing the people as Your duty. Wherever Heaven covers and [earth] bears, there is not a single man who does not fulfill the joy of plowing, eating, and drinking; wherever the sun and moon [shine] and frost and dew fall, there is not a single person who does not fulfill the [virtues?] of paternal kindness and filial piety. Governance is already pervasive, yet You still worry that it is not pervasive enough; the people are already at peace, yet You still worry that they are not peaceful enough. Now You have further brought Your servants before the Court and asked about instruction and nourishment in the eras of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. Your servant knows that this heart of Your Majesty is none other than the heart of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu, desiring to make the people of today become like the people of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. How could Your servant dare not keep a pure and devoted heart to respond to and extol the glorious mandate of the Sacred Son of Heaven?
Looking back at the ruler of Yu [Shun], who continued the governance of Taotang [Yao]: worrying that the common people were suffering from hunger, he appointed Ji [Houji] to the office of Director of Agriculture (Tianzheng) to sow the hundred grains in season, so that all the people might obtain their nourishment; worrying that the common people were not affectionate toward one another, he appointed Xie to take charge of the office of Minister of Education (Situ) to reverently propagate the Five Teachings, so that all the people might restore their innate nature. 太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸統一六合掃胡元之弊政興

translation_en: … the black-haired people were transformed, and the myriad states enjoyed the efficacy of universal peace. As for the Three Dynasties arising in succession, to speak of their land systems: the Xia dynasty allotted fifty mu of land to each adult male, calculating the yield of five mu from each man as tribute (gong). The Shang people first established the well-field system, dividing six hundred and thirty mu of land into nine plots of seventy mu each; the center was the public field, while on the outside eight families were each allotted one plot, merely borrowing their labor to help cultivate the public field without further taxing their private fields, which was therefore called aid (zhu). The Zhou people allotted one hundred mu and used the彻 (che, "sharing") system: the suburban districts and outlying regions used the tribute method, while the capital domains and borderlands used the aid method, combining their strength to work together when plowing and dividing the harvest equally according to acreage when reaping. Although the systems of their fields were different, the way they enriched the people's livelihood was the same. To speak of their schools: the Xia called them the Eastern Hall (Dongxu) and Western Hall (Xixu); the Yin called them the Left School (Zuoxue) and Right School (Youxue); by the Zhou, the regulations became even more detailed. The first was called [□□] [Shangxiang, the Upper School?], which was a虞 [or Xia] school; entertaining the state elders and reading books in winter took place there. The second was called [□□] [Dongxu, the Eastern Hall?], which was a [□□] [Xia school?]; entertaining the commoner elders, learning shield and halberd dances in spring and summer, learning feather and flute dances in秋冬, and engaging in discourse and explanation upon reaching completeness at fifteen all took place there. The third was called the Hall of the Blind Musicians (Guzong), which was a Yin school; sacrificing to the ancestors of music, chanting in spring, playing stringed instruments in summer, and studying ritual in autumn took place there. The fourth was called the Circular Moat (Biyong) for the Son of Heaven and the Semicircular Moat (Pangong) for the feudal lords, which was a Zhou school located in the suburbs; making sacrificial offerings to the former teachers, receiving sacrificial meat when setting out on military expeditions, and reporting back and presenting the severed ears of the slain upon returning took place there. The fifth was called the Hall of Equal Perfection (Chengjun), which was shared by all four dynasties. Although the names of their schools were not uniform, the way they clarified human moral relations was one and the same. At that time, the millions of people truly multiplied and flourished, and every household had customs worthy of enfeoffment. 皆有田輕徭薄賦敦本尚實所以養之者厚矣
首務建學而民皆有造躬行實踐建中立極所
以教之者至矣歌鳳儀獸舞之治者咸囿於春
風和氣之中樂魚躍鳶飛之化者咸席於景星
慶雲之下其治效之隆與唐虞三代同一揆也
太宗文皇帝中興家邦
仁宗昭皇帝恭己守成農事之重心乎

translation_en:
…all had fields; labor service was lightened and taxes were reduced, emphasizing agriculture and valuing practical substance—thus the means of nourishing them were generous indeed. He made establishing schools the foremost task so that the people might all achieve accomplishment, practicing what he preached in person and establishing the supreme standard of the Mean—thus the means of educating them were utmost indeed. Those who sang of a rule in which phoenixes came in stately manner and beasts danced were all embraced within the genial air of spring breezes; those who rejoiced in the transforming influence under which fishes leaped and hawks soared were all seated beneath auspicious stars and felicitous clouds. The splendor of the efficacy of his rule followed the very same principles as Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties.

Emperor Taizong Wen brought about a dynastic revival of the state, and Emperor Renzong Zhao maintained the accomplishments of his predecessors with reverent self-restraint. In the emphasis placed on agriculture, their minds were at one with the minds of the Two Sages [?]; in the exaltation of educational administration, they modeled themselves on the laws of the Two Sages [?]. The ancestors shared a single mind, […?] earnestly continuing and setting forth their legacy, taking their minds as Your own mind [?] and modeling Your governance on the governance of the Sages [?].

The system of land tenure strictly adheres to the established constitutions, yet the administration of encouraging and supervising agriculture grows ever more diligent, and edicts remitting land taxes have been repeatedly handed down. The schools strictly follow the old statutes, yet the methods of encouragement and supervision are invariably rigorous, and the ways of educating and nourishing grow ever more refined. When putting on clothing, You think of the cold suffered by the people; when taking food, You think of the hunger suffered by the people—Your love for the people has the sincerity of protecting a newborn infant. Leading the people first with filial piety and fraternal submission, and guiding the people with rites and music—Your moral transformation is rooted in the reality of personal practice.

As for regional governors and prefects, upon whom the weal and woe of the common people depend, You invariably select talents like those of Gong Sui 龔遂, Huang Ba 黃霸, Zhuo Mao 卓茂, and Lu Gong 魯恭 to occupy those posts. As for exemplar-teachers, upon whom the flourishing or decline of moral customs hinges, You invariably select those with the learning of Hu Yuan 胡瑗…

text:
程頤之學以任之是皆
皇上已行之政已驗之效猶且曰田里未皆給足風
俗未底刑措欲臣舉要以對臣又知
皇上謙退不足之心即大舜好問好察大禹不自滿
假之心也臣惟為政固在於用人之當得人尤
在於考核之公何則選曹乃人物之銓衡風憲
為百司之表率使居是任者誠能秉至公之心
擇適用之才精練並博采既已得而任之而又循

punctuated: 程頤之學以任之。是皆皇上已行之政、已驗之效，猶且曰：「田里未皆給足，風俗未底刑措。」欲臣舉要以對，臣又知皇上謙退不足之心，即大舜好問好察、大禹不自滿假之心也。臣惟為政固在於用人之當，得人尤在於考核之公。何則？選曹乃人物之銓衡，風憲為百司之表率，使居是任者誠能秉至公之心，擇適用之才，精練並博采，既已得而任之，而又循名責實，以行勸懲黜陟之典。嚴敕之，則任教養之職者，□而益闢，何患民之未足？風由是而益厚，何患刑之未措哉？臣學不足以明體適用，才不足以博古通今，謹以是為獻。伏惟皇上萬幾之暇，少垂睿覽。臣謹對。
translation_en:
… and Cheng Yi 程頤 to appoint to them. These are all policies that Your Majesty has already implemented and results that have already been proven effective, yet You still say: "The fields and villages are not yet all adequately supplied, and moral customs have not yet reached the point where punishments can be set aside," and wish Your servant to summarize the essentials in reply. From this Your servant further knows that Your Majesty's humble and self-effacing mind, never considering itself sufficient, is none other than the mind of Great Shun 大舜, who loved to ask and loved to examine, and of Great Yu 大禹, who was free from self-satisfaction and arrogance.

Your servant reflects that while governance indeed lies in the proper employment of men, obtaining the right men lies even more in the impartiality of their evaluation. Why is this so? The Ministry of Personnel (選曹) is the balance scale for weighing human talent, and the Censorate (風憲) is the exemplar for all the hundred offices. If those who occupy these posts can truly uphold a mind of utmost impartiality, select talents suited for practical application, and combine rigorous training with broad recruitment; and once having obtained and appointed them, furthermore require that their actual performance match their nominal duties in order to carry out the statutory canons of encouragement, warning, demotion, and promotion—and if You strictly command them [?], then those who hold the offices of instruction and nourishment will […], and the land will thereby be increasingly opened up [?]; what worry then would there be that the people are not yet adequately supplied? Moral customs will thereby become increasingly generous; what worry then would there be that punishments are not yet set aside?

Your servant's learning is insufficient to illuminate fundamental principles and apply them to practical use, and his talent is insufficient to encompass both antiquity and the present; he respectfully offers this up. Humbly praying that Your Majesty, in moments of leisure from myriad affairs of state, will deign to cast Your imperial gaze upon it, Your servant respectfully replies.
